extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and scholars interested in peer review, publication bias, and scientific evaluation (especially in psychology/behavioral sciences)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines, experimental measures, and evaluative criteria used by journal referees to judge submitted research manuscripts (components, rating dimensions, and recommendation decisions). Focused on how reviewers weight introduction, methods, results, and discussion and on sources of bias in those judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript components to be evaluated (introduction, methodology, results, interpretation/discussion, abstract, bibliography)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most research publications are viewed as composed of an introduction, a description of experimental methodology, a summary of results, and an interpretation or discussion of the data; supplemented by an abstract and a bibliography these may constitute the sole basis for reviewers' recommendations (especially under blind review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reviewers should consider each component; the study manipulated these components (present/absent/ambiguous) to assess their influence. Note examples where missing components produced reviewer awkwardness and qualified reviews ('assuming that the Discussion is reasonable').

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Rating of the manuscript's relevance and importance (one of five explicit rating factors used by the Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis in the experiment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured on a 4-point rating scale; in the experiment topic relevance did not differ across conditions (average rating high). Reviewers should evaluate whether the research question addresses an important problem; ideally this should be judged independently of outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the adequacy and rigor of the experimental procedures and design (explicit rating factor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated on a 4-point scale (poor, marginal, adequate, good). The paper argues methodology should be a primary basis for editorial decisions (should outrank outcome); but findings show reviewers' methodology ratings were biased by the direction of reported results (halo effect). Reviewers should check internal consistency (e.g., detect contradictory sample-size statements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of how results are presented (tables, figures, clarity, labeling) — an explicit rating factor in the experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated on a 4-point scale. The study shows data presentation ratings were influenced by whether results supported reviewers' perspectives. Guidance: presentation quality should be judged on clarity and accuracy, independent of whether data confirm theory; pay attention to correct labeling of curves/tables to avoid misleading interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion / Interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge the quality, logic, and appropriateness of the discussion and interpretation of the data (explicit rating factor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should not allow an author's discussion to unduly bias publication recommendations; editors may request authors to publicly recognize alternate interpretations. In the experiment the presence and valence of the discussion influenced perceptions of ambiguous data in some groups but generally did not override data- or method-based judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall scientific contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: A global assessment of the manuscript's contribution to the field (explicit rating factor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated on a 4-point scale. The study found positive-result manuscripts were rated as having higher scientific contribution than negative-result papers; removing results sometimes led to higher contribution ratings than when negative results were present. Guidance: contribution should be based on relevance and methodological adequacy, not merely outcome direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary recommendation (acceptance decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single summary recommendation intended to aid editorial decision: accept, accept with minor revisions, accept with major revisions, or reject (4-point summary scale used by the journal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was treated as the critical dependent variable in the experiment. Reviewers used a 4-point recommendation scale; identical manuscripts received different recommendations depending on reported outcome (positive manuscripts tended toward acceptance with moderate revisions; negative ones toward rejection or major revision). Nonparametric statistics may be needed when variances differ across groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind reviewing / reviewer anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure where referees are unaware of authorship and institutional affiliation; under blind review the manuscript components may be the sole basis for judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blind review is intended to reduce biases based on prestige/affiliation. The experiment used blind procedures to isolate the influence of manuscript content (results & discussion) on reviewers' evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer weighting introduction and methodology over results and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Epistemological ideal: given a relevant research question and adequate methodology, the obtained results—whatever they might be—should be of interest; thus introduction and methods should outrank results and discussion in evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues for a falsificational logic (negative results often more informative) and suggests that reviewers should prioritize relevance and methodological adequacy. Practical suggestion investigated: have referees evaluate relevance/methodology without seeing results or interpretation to reduce confirmatory bias — though this raises other problems (e.g., low inter-reviewer agreement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confirmatory bias (do not favor positive/confirmatory results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluators should not be prejudiced toward manuscripts that report results consistent with their theoretical perspective; negative (contratheoretical) results should not be penalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The experiment demonstrates strong bias against manuscripts reporting results contrary to reviewers' perspectives. Remedies discussed include blinded evaluation of relevance/methodology (without results) and training — but training may produce consensus built on shared biases. The normative claim: negative results carry stronger logical implications (Popper) and ought to be valued accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rating scale design and anchors
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of explicit rating scales and anchors for component ratings (in the study: 4-point scale with anchors poor, marginal, adequate, good).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly defined scales support measurement and statistical analysis of reviewer judgments. The study used such scales for five factors and a separate 4-point recommendation scale; design considerations include handling non-homogeneous variances and choosing appropriate statistical tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater agreement / reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of consistency among reviewers (intraclass correlation coefficients reported for each factor; self-predicted reliability compared to obtained reliability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review should be treated as an evaluative test requiring evidence of reliability (APA analogy). The experiment found low inter-referee agreement on many factors (e.g., relevance ICC = -.07), highlighting the need to measure and report reviewer reliability and consider methods to improve it (training, clearer criteria), while noting training can introduce shared bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of reviews (deadline adherence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether reviewers return evaluations by stated deadlines (45 days in the experiment) and the relation of punctuality to evaluation outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured in the study (percent returned by deadline). Findings: mixed-results manuscripts were returned earlier; punctual reviews were marginally more negative. Editors should monitor timeliness and consider its potential association with review stringency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of internal inconsistencies / attention to detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers' ability to notice contradictions or errors within the manuscript (e.g., inconsistent sample-size statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The experiment found detection rates varied by condition (reviewers seeing negative results noted contradictions more often). Attention to internal consistency is an important quality-control criterion and can be influenced by reviewer biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructiveness and substantive depth of reviewer comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of open-ended comments, suggestions, and supplemental materials provided by reviewers (e.g., bibliographies, reprints, analyses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many reviewers provided lengthy, constructive comments; editors should value substantive feedback (even when critical). The study documents examples of helpful behavior (sending related reprints, performing analyses) and notes reviewers often qualified comments when components were missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of ambiguous or mixed results
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of manuscripts with equivocal/mixed data and how the framing/interpretation (positive vs negative discussion) affects recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The experiment created ambiguous results and paired them with opposing discussions; mixed-results manuscripts were consistently rejected in this study, and the discussion section had limited influence. Guidance: reviewers should carefully assess ambiguity (consider altitude vs slope interpretations) and avoid allowing interpretive framing to override objective assessment of methods and data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review as evaluative testing: require evidence of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy that peer review functions like a psychological test and therefore should be held to standards of reliability and validity (the APA recommends reporting indices of reliability and validity for tests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper recommends developing and reporting psychometric evidence for reviewer instruments/processes (e.g., inter-rater reliability, construct validity) before assuming peer review is 'naturally' reliable and objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial prerogative and separate evaluation of missing components
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors may evaluate missing manuscript components separately and use editorial prerogative to request authors to address interpretation alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the experiment, referees were told missing parts were 'in preparation' and to evaluate the manuscript's present merits; editors should be explicit about how incomplete submissions will be handled and may solicit separate reviews for delayed components.
